title: Delay is the cure
hook: the best cure for anger is delay (On Anger 2.29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: brief madness, anger in the mirror. Your line was brief madness. Where did your early-warning sign show up, and did you name it? Day five hundred four, the end of a week.

The email arrives at 4:52 on a Friday. It's unfair, it's wrong, and it copies your boss. Your fingers are already typing. The reply is excellent. It's sharp, it's true, it would feel wonderful to send. Replies like that get written every day. Some get sent. Yesterday Seneca named anger: a brief madness. Today, deep in his second book, he gives what he calls the greatest remedy for it, and it's almost disappointingly simple. Not a technique. Not a philosophy. Just time. Today: delay is the cure.
screen: `4:52 ON A FRIDAY.` → `THE REPLY IS EXCELLENT.` → `SENECA'S GREATEST REMEDY: TIME.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The greatest remedy for anger, Seneca says, is delay. Ask anger for time, not so that it will forgive, but so that it can judge. Its first rush is heavy; if it waits, it eases. You don't have to win the argument with anger. You just have to outlast its first wave. Second, don't try to remove it all at once. Seneca is realistic. Trying to rip anger out by force, in the first moment, rarely works. Picking it apart a little at a time does. Wait, and the parts loosen. Third, while you wait, judge. Seneca says much of our anger rests on things we believed too quickly: a rumor, a look, a tone of voice in a message. Delay gives you time to ask the other side, to check the facts, to wonder whether there's a story you don't know. An angry reply can collapse under one question. Fourth, a teacher we've met. Remember Athenodorus, who advised serving where you can? Possibly the same man; some readers think so. The later writer Plutarch says that when Athenodorus left the court of the emperor Augustus, his parting advice was: when you're angry, don't say or do anything until you've recited the alphabet to yourself. Twenty-four Greek letters. That's a delay you can carry anywhere. And our week, looking back: calm is catching, less to lose, read, don't display, minds need play, finish the game, brief madness. Seneca's tools are rarely dramatic. A friend, a plain shelf, a game, a breath, and now, a pause.
screen: `THE GREATEST REMEDY IS DELAY.` · `NOT ALL AT ONCE.` · `WAIT, THEN JUDGE.` · `ATHENODORUS: RECITE THE ALPHABET.` · then, large: `DELAY.`

segments.voice: Think of a reply you're tempted to send, or a conversation you're tempted to have, while you're still hot. Picture writing it. Now picture not sending it. Put it in a drawer, a draft folder, an envelope. Notice what the waiting is like. Itchy? Unfinished? A little relieved? Breathe through it. While you breathe, ask one question you skipped: what might I not know about this? The bell holds the time.
Delay is the cure. Seneca's greatest remedy for anger: give it time, not to forgive, but to judge. Its first rush passes. Today's word.
Your line: delay. The next time a reply comes hot, wait one hour before you send it. If an hour is impossible, recite the alphabet first. Day five hundred four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca set a rule to wait before acting or replying in anger, sometimes an hour, sometimes a night, to let the first rush pass.

fork.setup: an unfair email arrives on Friday afternoon, copying your boss. your reply is ready. what does Seneca's remedy say?
options: wait; let the first rush pass, then judge.
fork.reveal: delay, he says, is the greatest remedy: anger's first wave is heavy and passes if it waits.

original.note: Latin, 'delay': Seneca's greatest remedy for anger.

trapdoor: what you thought: delay means suppressing your anger.
what it means: delay gives anger time to judge; its first rush passes, and facts can be checked.
what a scholar hears: Seneca gives the delay remedy more than once in On Anger (at 2.29 and again at 3.12); the alphabet story comes from Plutarch's Sayings of Romans, not from Seneca.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): softened 'every one of us has a folder', 'single best answer' (now Seneca's own 'greatest remedy'), 'many angry replies', and 'most likely the same man' (Athenodorus identity is uncertain); practice and howItsDone no longer tell the listener what they feel or what 'many people' do; added On Anger 3.12 to sources for the trapdoor.

On Anger 2.29 paraphrased: delay as the greatest remedy; ask it of anger to judge, not to pardon; first assault heavy; don't try to remove it all at once. Confirm whether the Latin at 2.29 is 'dilatio' or 'mora' (3.12.4 has 'maximum remedium irae mora est'); the original game uses 'mora'.
On Anger 2.22–24: don't believe quickly; hear the other side. Confirm.

Plutarch, Moralia 207C (Sayings of Romans, Augustus 7): Athenodorus' advice to recite the 24 letters of the alphabet before acting in anger. Confirm the identity link with Seneca's Athenodorus (day 497) is presented as 'we've met' and is plausible but not certain.
Week look-back (days 498–503) uses those days' carries.
